Spinal Mechanics & Thoracic Spine

OMM I — Summary #2

Type II flexed vs. extended facet mechanics, T1–T2 (source: fitness-vip.com/muscle-chains/fryettes-laws)

Fryette's Principles for Diagnosis

  • Type I (neutral) dysfunctions: involve 3 or more spinal levels
  • Type II (F/E) dysfunctions: involve ONE spinal level
Flexed (Type II)
  • One facet is stuck in an open position
  • Segment rotates & sidebends AWAY from the open facet when extended
  • OMT goal → close the open facet
Extended (Type II)
  • One facet is stuck in a closed position
  • Segment rotates & sidebends TOWARDS the closed facet when flexed
  • OMT goal → open the closed facet
Relative motion: the vertebra directly below the level of the somatic dysfunction has the exact opposite motion of the dysfunctional vertebra. E.g., T1FSLRL · T2ESRRR

Of note: only non-neutral dysfunctions (Type II — F/E) apply to the cervical spine — meaning the cervical spine has NO Type I dysfunctions like the thoracic and lumbar spine do.

Predominant Spinal Motions

RegionPredominant Motion
Occipitoatlantal (OA)Flexion / Extension
Atlantoaxial (AA)Rotation (40–50% of total c-spine rotation)
Typical Cervical Vertebrae (C2–C7)Mainly Flexion/Extension + some sidebending
Thoracic Vertebrae (T1–T12)Mainly Rotation + some sidebending
Lumbar Vertebrae (L1–L5)Mainly Flexion/Extension + sidebending, with minor rotation

“BUM, BUL, BM”

Cervical Spine

OMM I — Summary #3

Anatomy Review

  • 8 cervical nerve roots — all exit superior to their named vertebra, except C8, which exits inferior to C7
  • Each transverse foramen contains an artery, vein, and nerve — vulnerable to shearing forces

Fryette's Mechanics Do NOT Apply to the Cervical Spine

  • No Type I / Type II dysfunctions
  • Rotation and sidebending are coupled to the SAME side for typical cervical vertebrae (C2–C7)
  • Motion is governed by facet joint orientation (“BUM”) and the uncovertebral joints (Joints of Luschka)
  • Uncovertebral joints and uncinate processes are found ONLY in the typical cervical vertebrae (C2–C7)
Occipitoatlantal (OA): C0–C1
  • Rotation and sidebending in opposite directions
  • “OA” = “Opposite Always”
  • Governed by 2 articulations: occipital condyles (convex) + superior facets of atlas (concave, converge anteriorly)
  • Possible diagnoses: OA FSRRL, OA FSLRR, OA ESRRL, OA ESLRR (always opposite)
Atlantoaxial (AA): C1–C2
  • Governed by 4 articulations: right + left zygapophyseal joints, plus 2 involving the dens (odontoid process), which acts as the pivot around which the atlas rotates
  • DDx by flexing the cervical spine to at least 45°
  • Possible diagnoses: AA RR, AA RL

Typical Cervical Vertebrae (C2–C7)

  • Uncovertebral joints are synovial joints on the lateral aspect of the vertebral bodies, formed by the uncinate processes of 2 adjacent vertebrae
  • They protect the intervertebral disc from herniation/blunt trauma in a posterolateral direction
Possible findings: CX FRSR, CX FRSL, CX ERSR, CX ERSL (X = 2–7) — rotation & sidebending same side, per the coupling rule above
Uncinate process & uncovertebral joint (source: chegg.com flashcards)
Joint of Luschka, intervertebral foramen & articular processes (source: neupsykey.com)

Pelvis

OMM Summary #10

Gait Cycle + Pelvis

  • As the leg flexes (swing phase), the ipsilateral innominate rotates posteriorly (and flares out)
  • As the leg extends (stance phase), the ipsilateral innominate rotates anteriorly (and flares in)

7 Axes of Sacral Motion on the Ilia

#AxisNotes
1Vertical axis
2Right oblique axis
3Respiratory (superior transverse) axisS1 — primary respiratory motions
4Sacroiliac (middle transverse) axisS2 — postural motion of the sacrum; sacrum rotates around this axis
5Iliosacral (inferior transverse) axisS3 — iliosacral motion; innominates rotate around this axis
6Left oblique axis
7Anteroposterior axis
7 axes of sacral motion, marked on the pelvis (top, posterior view) and sacrum (bottom, lateral view) — axis 1 (vertical) and axis 7 (anteroposterior) shown running through both

Pelvic SD Diagnosis Sequence

1Laterality (left vs. right)
  • Both the Standing Flexion Test and ASIS Compression Test tell you the same thing and should correlate — if they don't, choose whichever is more obviously dysfunctional and lateralize to that side
  • Standing Flexion Test: physician thumbs wrap to the inferior aspects of the PSIS. The PSIS that moves first and farthest, or last and longest = the positive (dysfunctional) side
  • ASIS Compression Test: compress each innominate (ASIS) one at a time with a posterior-inferior vector, monitoring the contralateral ASIS for motion — engages the iliosacral (inferior transverse) axis. E.g., right side is positive if compressing the right ASIS causes the left ASIS to be immediately felt rotating (no delay)
2Landmarks
  • Focus on landmarks on the positive (dysfunctional) side and compare to the other side: ASIS, pubic tubercles, and PSIS
  • Determine if landmarks on the (+) side are superior or inferior compared to the other side
  • Also check if ASIS is medial or lateral (for flare)

Pelvic Somatic Dysfunctions

Pubic Dysfunctions
1Superior pubic shear
2Inferior pubic shear
3Pubic compression
Iliosacral / Innominate Dysfunctions
1Anteriorly rotated innominate
2Posteriorly rotated innominate
3Superior innominate shear
4Inferior innominate shear
5Innominate Inflare (rotated medially)
6Innominate Outflare (rotated laterally)

Sacrum

OMM Summary #11

Motion of the Sacrum

  • Flexion/Extension occur around a transverse axis
  • Sidebending occurs around a transverse axis
  • Rotation occurs around a vertical axis
  • Torsion occurs around an oblique axis — named for the superior aspect the axis passes through

Sacral SD Diagnosis Sequence

1AGR Screen
2Laterality (left vs. right)
  • Seated Flexion Test — feet flat on the floor. PSIS that moves first & farthest, or last & longest = positive (dysfunctional) side
  • ASIS Compression Test — posterior and slightly medial vector, engages the sacroiliac (middle transverse) axis. E.g., right side positive if compressing right ASIS causes left ASIS to be immediately felt rotating (no delay)
3Spring Test (anterior vs. posterior)
  • Physician hand on the sacral base, near the lumbosacral junction (patient may or may not be on elbows)
  • Anterior force to the sacral base should induce flexion of the sacrum
  • Positive test — NO spring = Posterior (backward-going / extended) dysfunction
  • Negative test — spring felt = Anterior (forward-going / flexed) dysfunction
4Static Landmarks (sacral sulci and ILAs)
  • Determine if landmarks are anterior/deep or posterior/shallow compared to the other side
5Sphynx Test (anterior vs. posterior)
  • Monitor all 4 landmarks while the patient induces sacral flexion (comes up onto elbows from prone)
  • Increased symmetry = forward-going sacrum
  • Decreased / unchanged symmetry = backward-going sacrum
6Motion Testing — MOST RELIABLE TEST
  • Posterior-to-anterior pressure applied over all four corners (one at a time), checking for ease of motion

L5 Rule (Sacral Torsions) — “ROSSA”

L5 “Rotated Opposite, Sidebent Same Axis”
  • E.g., L on R → L5 FRRSR
  • Forward torsions = Neutral L5 (Type 1)
  • Backward torsions = Non-Neutral (flexed) L5 (Type 2)

Gait Cycle + Sacrum

  • Stance phase = ipsilateral oblique axis
  • Swing phase = anterior oblique motion around that axis
  • Sacroiliac motion is caused by vertebral column position changes
  • Iliosacral motion is caused by leg movement

Sacral Somatic Dysfunctions

Original source table — Sacral Somatic Dysfunctions (sacroiliac/sacral shears + torsions)
Sacral Shears (Sacroiliac / Sacral Dysfunctions)
1Bilaterally flexed sacrum
2Bilaterally extended sacrum
3Unilaterally flexed sacrum (a. R, b. L)
4Unilaterally extended sacrum (a. R, b. L)
Sacral Torsions
5Forward sacral torsion (a. L on L, b. R on R)

Sacral Diagnosis Algorithm & ME Treatments

Full stepwise pathway from lateralization to specific torsion/shear diagnosis, plus the muscle energy (ME) technique for each — source: Sacral Diagnosis Algorithm & ME Treatments

Original algorithm diagram, reproduced in full — use this as the primary reference; the walkthrough below explains it in prose
1Positive Lateralization Test
  • Seated Flexion Test
  • ASIS Compression Test (SI axis)

Result: lateralizes the dysfunction to LEFT or RIGHT.

2Sphynx / Spring Test — determines the pattern

If the Seated Flexion Test is negative AND the ASIS Compression Test is bilaterally positive, this points to a bilateral (non-lateralized) pattern instead:

  • POSITIVE Spring Test = Bilateral Extension (EX-EX-EX)
  • NEGATIVE Spring Test = Bilateral Flexion (IN-IN-IN)

If a side did lateralize (left or right), the Sphynx/Spring test result differentiates a torsion (oblique axis, named by the DOWN-UP-DOWN / DOWN-DOWN-DOWN / UP-UP-UP pattern) from a unilateral shear (named EX-EX-EX or IN-IN-IN on that side alone). The diagram pairs this with small landmark grids (sacral sulcus depth "D" vs. the ILA "A" finding) for each of the four possible diagnoses per side — see the embedded image above for the exact grid orientation, since it's easiest to read directly off the original rather than transcribed.

3Resulting Diagnoses, By Lateralized Side

If lateralized LEFT:

  • Left on Right (torsion) — DOWN-UP-DOWN
  • Left on Left (torsion) — DOWN-DOWN-DOWN or UP-UP-UP
  • Left unilaterally Extended — EX-EX-EX
  • Left unilaterally Flexed — IN-IN-IN

If lateralized RIGHT:

  • Right on Left (torsion) — DOWN-UP-DOWN
  • Right on Right (torsion) — DOWN-DOWN-DOWN or UP-UP-UP
  • Right unilaterally Extended — EX-EX-EX
  • Right unilaterally Flexed — IN-IN-IN
Quick relational notes from the source algorithm:
Backward/Extended Sacrum = Flexed L5  ·  Forward/Flexed Sacrum = Neutral L5

ME Technique Reference — What Each Pattern Name Means

DOWN-UP-DOWN
  1. Sacral oblique axis down
  2. Patient face up (supine)
  3. Physician applies force down
DOWN-DOWN-DOWN
  1. Sacral oblique axis down
  2. Patient face down (Sim's position)
  3. Physician applies force down
UP-UP-UP
  1. Sacral oblique axis up
  2. Patient face up (supine)
  3. Physician applies force up
IN-IN-IN
  1. Abduct and internally rotate the leg(s)
  2. Contact the inferior lateral angle(s)
  3. Patient inhales; physician holds the sacrum in extension
  4. Resist flexion during exhalation
EX-EX-EX
  1. Patient extends the lumbar spine
  2. Abduct and externally rotate the leg(s)
  3. Contact the sacral base(s)
  4. Patient exhales; physician holds the sacrum in flexion
  5. Resist extension during inhalation

Shoulder

OMM I — Summary #4

Shoulder Girdle (Clavicle + Scapula)

Part of the appendicular skeleton that anchors the upper extremity to the axial skeleton.

Shoulder Joints

JointKey Features
Sternoclavicular (SC)Saddle joint — motion in 3 planes; costoclavicular ligament (CCL) is the fulcrum for the clavicle; the ONLY true joint connecting the arm to the axial skeleton
Acromioclavicular (AC)Prone to separation/injury from torn ligaments (SITS ligaments)
Glenohumeral (GH)Most mobile but LEAST stable joint — prone to dislocations; glenoid labrum deepens the glenoid cavity to help keep the humeral head in the fossa
Scapulothoracic ArticulationA pseudo-joint

Scapulohumeral Rhythm

The degrees of motion for the scapula and humerus are in a 1:2 ratio. For example, when abducting the upper extremity to 180°: 60° comes from scapular upward rotation, and 120° comes from humeral abduction at the shoulder joint.

Scapulohumeral rhythm — 60° scapular rotation : 120° humeral rotation for 180° total abduction

Shoulder / Clavicle Diagnosis

  • Shoulder is named for RESTRICTION. The shoulder and the hips are the ONLY SDs you name for restriction, NOT ease. E.g., “Right shoulder restricted in flexion”
  • Clavicle is named for restricted SIDE, but the motion of EASE. E.g., “Left superior clavicular head” means the left clavicle is more restricted compared to the right, but its ease of motion is superior (i.e., it's restricted to inferior motion)

Apley's Scratch Test (quick shoulder ROM screen)

ArmMotions Tested
Top armFlexion, External Rotation, Abduction
Bottom armExtension, Internal Rotation, Adduction
Shoulder Shrug
  • Tests superior/inferior motion of the clavicle
  • Patient supine, physician monitors the superior aspect of the SC joint, patient brings shoulders toward ears
  • Clavicular head doesn't move inferior (named for restricted side) ⇒ “superior clavicular head” (ease of motion)
Shrug test axis of motion (superior/inferior clavicle)
“Zombie Arms”
  • Tests anterior/posterior motion of the clavicle
  • Patient supine, physician monitors the anterior aspect of the SC joint, patient raises arms toward the ceiling
  • Clavicular head doesn't move posterior (named for restricted side) ⇒ “ant. clavicular head” (ease of motion)
Zombie arms axis of motion (anterior/posterior clavicle)

Elbow & Wrist

OMM I — Summary #5

Elbow Stability Assessment

Stabilize the distal forearm.

TestTechniqueTests
Varus Stress TestLateral force on the medial humerusRadial collateral ligament
Valgus Stress TestMedial force on the lateral humerusUlnar collateral ligament
Varus stress test
Valgus stress test

Parallelogram Mechanics

The interosseous membrane transmits force from the distal radius to the ulna and vice versa.

  • ABduction of distal ulna = medial glide at olecranon (proximal) = ADducted wrist
  • ADduction of distal ulna = lateral glide at olecranon (proximal) = ABducted wrist
Parallelogram mechanics — ulnar abduction
Parallelogram mechanics — ulnar adduction

Ulna — SD Named for Ease of Distal End

Screen with carrying angle, then motion test.

  • Abducted ulna = distal end more lateral; olecranon prefers medial glide
  • Adducted ulna = distal end more medial; olecranon prefers lateral glide

Wrist — SD Name Based on Ease & Anatomic Position

  • Carpal bones glide Anterior — ease in glide toward the palm
  • Carpal bones glide Posterior — ease in glide toward the dorsum
Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: compression of the median nerve at the carpal tunnel (flexor retinaculum) of the wrist.

Radius — SD Named for Ease of Proximal End (Head)

“SAPP”: Supination brings radial head Anterior · Pronation brings radial head Posterior
  • Anterior radial head prefers supination
  • Posterior radial head prefers pronation

Falling Onto an OutStretched Hand (FOOSH)

Fall DirectionHand PositionResult
Falling forward (arm flexed, landing on palm)Pronated during fallPronated forearm = posterior motion of radial head → posterior radial head
Falling backward (arm extended, landing on palm)Supinated during traumaSupinated forearm = anterior motion of radial head → anterior radial head

Epicondylitis

ConditionLocationCause
Lateral Epicondylitis — “tennis elbow”Tenderness at the origin of the extensor tendon of the wrist / lateral elbowRepetitive wrist extension with supination/pronation
Medial Epicondylitis — “golfer's elbow”Tenderness at the origin of the flexor tendon of the wrist / medial elbowRepetitive wrist flexion and pronation

Lower Extremity Overview

OMM Summary #9

SD Diagnosis, By Structure

StructureHow It's DiagnosedExample
HipPassive ROM bilaterally while stabilizing the contralateral ASIS (isolates hip ROM). SD named for the RESTRICTED ROM“Right hip restriction to flexion” / “Right hip resists flexion”
TibiaStabilize femur, rotate tibia internally & externally testing ease of motion (seated or supine w/ knee slightly flexed)“Internally rotated left tibia”
Fibular HeadFlex knee to ~90°, stabilize tibia, glide fibular head anterolaterally & posteromedially for ease (if supine, sit on the patient's foot, not the ankle)“Anterior left fibular head”
Lateral MalleolusAssess ease of anterior/posterior glide on the tibia — moves opposite the fibular head (usually)“Posterior right lateral malleolus”
Talocrural (Ankle) JointAssess ease of anterior/posterior glide of the talus on the tibia with plantarflexion/dorsiflexion“Anterior right talus” (prefers PF) · “Posterior left talus” (prefers DF)
Subtalar JointAssess ease of inversion/eversion of the calcaneus on the talus“Inverted right calcaneus” · “Everted left calcaneus”
Tarsal Bones (cuboid, navicular, cuneiforms)Assess ease of plantar (inferior) / dorsal (superior) glide of individual tarsal bones“Superior right cuboid bone” · “Inferior left navicular bone”
Metatarsals & PhalangesStabilize the proximal part of each joint, assess ease of glide of the distal part (plantar/dorsal, lateral/medial, internal/external rotation)“Inferior left 1st metatarsal”

Knee

OMM I — Summary #6

Knee Basics

  • Compound joint: Tibiofemoral joint (2 condyles) + Patellofemoral joint
  • The tibiofibular joint is NOT part of the true knee joint
  • SDs of the knee are usually in minor motions: tibia externally rotates with knee extension; tibia internally rotates with knee flexion

Joint Locking / Screw Home Mechanism

  • At full extension, the knee passively locks due to medial rotation of the femoral condyles on the tibial plateau
  • The popliteus muscle laterally rotates the tibia to reverse this mechanism, or “unlock” the knee

The patella increases the efficiency of the quadriceps by lengthening the lever arm.

Genu Varum vs. Genu Valgum

DeformityCommon NameQ Angle
Genu Varum“Bow-legged”Decreased Q angle
Genu Valgum“Knocked-knees” — “Gum sticks the knees together”Increased Q angle

A large knee Q angle is a risk factor for patellar dislocation or subluxation. Women have larger Q angles.

Q angle of the knee — normal (<15°), knock-kneed/genu valgum (>20°), bow-legged/genu varum (<10°)

Fibular Head — SD Named for Ease

  • Fibular head moves opposite the lateral malleolus: “Anterior fibular head” = posterior lateral malleolus; “Posterior fibular head” = anterior lateral malleolus
  • Fibular head compression → severe restriction with minimal motion & lateral knee pain
  • Fibular head restrictions are common with hamstring strains & LCL injuries
Posterior fibular head is the most common peripheral nerve lesion of the lower extremity, causing compression of the common fibular (peroneal) nerve (L4–S2):
  • Paresthesia/numbness/loss of sensation of the lateral lower leg, dorsum of foot and toes (except the webbing between the 1st and 2nd toes)
  • Impaired eversion and dorsiflexion → foot drop, steppage gait

Meniscal Injury

ZoneBlood SupplyHealing
Lateral 1/3VascularGood healing
Medial 1/3AvascularBad healing
Knee anatomy — femur, patella, collateral & cruciate ligaments, menisci, tibia, fibula

Tibia — Gliding Motions (SD Named for Ease)

“Internally rotated tibia” · “Externally rotated tibia”

Ankle & Foot

OMM I — Summary #7

Ankle Motions

MotionDescriptionStrongest Muscle(s)
Plantarflexion (PF)“Pointed toes” — talus moves anteriorly on the tibiaTriceps surae (gastrocnemius + soleus)
Dorsiflexion (DF)“Flexed feet” — talus glides posteriorly under the tibiaTibialis anterior
AbductionLateral flexion of the foot—
AdductionMedial flexion of the foot—
InversionPlantar surface moves mediallyTibialis posterior (strongest inverter/adductor)
EversionPlantar surface moves laterallyFibularis longus & brevis (strongest evertors)
SupinationPF + ADduction + Inversion
PronationDF + ABduction + Eversion

Foot Joints

  • Talocalcaneal (Subtalar) Joint — inversion & adduction, eversion & abduction
  • Talocalcaneonavicular Joint
  • Calcaneocuboid Joint
  • Cuneonavicular Joint
  • Transverse Tarsal (Chopart's) Joint — inversion & eversion
  • Tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) Joints — allows the forefoot to invert/evert independent of the hindfoot
Foot joints — subtalar, transverse tarsal, intertarsal, tarsometatarsal, MTP & IP joints

Joints & Ligaments

  • Tibiofibular syndesmosis: Anterior Tibiofibular Ligament, Posterior Tibiofibular Ligament, Transverse Tibiofibular Ligament, Interosseous Ligament
  • Talotibial joint = the “true” ankle joint
  • Anterior Talofibular Ligament (ATF) — “Always Tears First”
  • Deltoid ligament — the medial ankle ligament; resists eversion & abduction/external rotation. Eversion ankle sprain → avulsion fracture of the medial malleolus
